Our workload is bursty: a small number of long-context inference requests (20–60k tokens) and a larger volume of short-chat queries and embeddings. Key questions:

- Memory vs throughput: where do we draw the line between H100 and A100 for the long requests?
- Can we use L4 for embeddings to save cost and still meet latency targets?
- What's the recommended reserve/burst split for a 12-month reserved commitment with expected 3x peak bursts per week?

I've attached a quick export of our last 30 days of telemetry (tokens per request, p95 latency). Can someone on your side provide a sensitivity recommendation and a short runbook we can include in our SOW?

Sergio — initial sensitivity workbook attached (SKU_sensitivity_workbook.xlsx). Notes below from the first-pass analysis after ingesting LongTail_SKU_Input.xlsx:

Quick summary (high level):
- H100: Best for long-context, memory-bound batches. If >40% of requests exceed ~32k tokens, H100s reduce tokenized OOM risk and improve tail latency. Cost per token is highest but unit latency for long requests is best.
- A100: Good balance for mixed workloads. For 8k–32k token tails, A100 with 80–96GB variants gives a pragmatic tradeoff of ~15–25% lower cost vs H100 for many customers while keeping predictable throughput.
- L4: Very cost-effective for short-context generation and embeddings. Latency is excellent for small contexts, but model quantization and memory limits make it unsuitable for >8k token requests.

Example sensitivity outputs (illustrative):
- Scenario A (memory-heavy): 60% long requests -> Recommend reserve 12 H100 slots + burst to 6 A100 for throughput smoothing.
- Scenario B (mixed): 30% long / 50% short / 20% embeddings -> Recommend reserve 10 A100 + 20 L4 for embeddings as separate pool; allow burst to 8 H100 for long peaks.
- Scenario C (throughput-heavy): 10% long / 80% short / 10% embeddings -> Recommend reserve primarily A100 + L4; H100 only for small canary pool.

Operational levers we modeled:
- Prefix/KV caching for repeated long-session users (saves ~20–40% token work).
- Eviction headroom settings and slot tiling (to avoid OOM on A100 when a few requests balloon).
- Canary pool with pinned H100 instances for known long-running flows.

I'll convert the workbook into a one-pager for Felicia; can someone confirm the concurrency numbers and whether embeddings run isolated? Also tagging potential cost delta estimates (tokens/$month) will require a rough baseline of monthly token volume.

Attachment: SKU_sensitivity_workbook.xlsx (xlsx)

Subject: Re: Dedicated SKU sensitivity for bursty workloads (LongTail AI)

Felicia — thanks for the data and for the patience. Attached is a concise summary (SKU_sensitivity_summary.pdf) and the workbook Priyom produced. High-level recommendation tailored to LongTail:

- Reserve recommendation (12-month SOW): Start with a 'tiered reserve' approach:
  - Reserve 10 x A100 (80–96GB) as the primary compute pool (balanced for mixed workloads).
  - Reserve 8 x L4 as a separate embedding pool (lower cost, better latency for small context embeds).
  - Keep a small pinned H100 canary pool (2 x H100) in the reserve for highest-memory tail requests and critical SLAs.

- Burst policy:
  - Allow burst access to up to 6 additional H100 slots during scheduled peaks; Redwood routing will prefer H100 for requests flagged as "long-context" and L4 for embedding/short requests.

- Why this mix:
  - A100 reserve reduces committed cost while handling most long-ish requests up to ~32k tokens with slot tiling and eviction policies.
  - H100s act as the safety valve for infrequent but very large long-context requests that would otherwise OOM and cause tail latency spikes.
  - L4 for embeddings preserves cost-efficiency and lower latency for short calls.

Operational next steps we propose:
1) Confirm concurrency for long-context requests (Priyom)
2) Redwood and LongTail to sign off on a canary plan (2 H100 reserve + policy for 2-week canary)
3) Procurement to review reserve counts and pricing; we'll draft amendment language for burst credits in the SOW.

I'll loop Kimberly (billing) and Soojin (ops) to help with procurement language and canary runbook.

Best,
Sergio Alvarez
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
sergio@redwood.com

Attachments: SKU_sensitivity_summary.pdf (pdf), SKU_sensitivity_workbook.xlsx (xlsx)
